name: Tamil Eelam
anchor: Kilinochchi, the LTTE administrative headquarters in northern Sri Lanka.
founder: Tamil United Liberation Front, then the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE)
laws: LTTE courts, civil police and boards in the areas it held
challenge: Sri Lanka captured the last LTTE-held land on 18 May 2009
recognition: No state has recognised it or its exile body
story:
Tamil Eelam is the name of an independent state that many Sri Lankan Tamils and their diaspora have sought in the north and east of Sri Lanka, an area of 18,880 square kilometres. In 1976 the Tamil United Liberation Front, a political party, adopted the Vaddukoddai Resolution calling for a free and sovereign state. In the 1977 election, on that promise, it won all 14 seats in the Northern Province and 4 of 10 in the Eastern Province. Sri Lanka's Sixth Amendment of 1983 then banned advocating a separate state.
The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), an armed group, went on to hold territory and run it much like a government. In those areas it had land, naval and air forces, local and higher courts, a civil police force, health and education boards, the Bank of Tamil Eelam, and radio and television stations. Kilinochchi was its administrative headquarters. The US State Department alleged that its judges had little training. In October 2003 the LTTE proposed an interim self-governing authority, which asked for regional autonomy in place of independence.
Government troops took Kilinochchi on 2 January 2009 and the last LTTE-held land on 18 May 2009. Almost all of the LTTE's leadership was killed, and tens of thousands of its fighters surrendered. In March 2010 the Tamil National Alliance, the main Tamil party, dropped the demand for independence in favour of federalism, a system in which a region keeps its own powers inside the country.
In May 2010 a New York lawyer, Visvanathan Rudrakumaran, formed the Transnational Government of Tamil Eelam among Tamils abroad. Diaspora votes on independence were held in ten countries in 2009 and 2010, including Norway, France and Canada. No state has recognised Tamil Eelam or this body, and the Sri Lankan government has called it a ploy to perpetuate terrorism.
mechanism: An armed group can run courts, police and a bank on land it holds without any state accepting it as a government. When the group lost the land, the working state ended, and the claim passed to a diaspora organisation with no territory.

name: Chechen Republic of Ichkeria
anchor: Grozny, its capital.
founder: Dzhokhar Dudayev and the All-National Congress of the Chechen People
currency: Russian ruble; a Chechen naxar is listed, but a note on the source says a planned currency never circulated
laws: Secular constitution of March 1992, later a sharia-based criminal code
challenge: Two wars with Russia; Grozny fell on 6 February 2000
recognition: No state now recognises it; the Taliban did in January 2000 and the exile government of Zviad Gamsakhurdia of Georgia did earlier
story:
The Chechen Republic of Ichkeria was a state that governed most of the former Checheno-Ingush region of the North Caucasus from 1991 to 2000, on about 15,300 square kilometres, with Grozny as its capital. Russia regarded the territory as its own throughout.
In June 1991 an All-National Congress of the Chechen People met in Grozny at the urging of Dzhokhar Dudayev, a Soviet air force general, as the Soviet Union was falling apart. Its armed squads seized the local KGB headquarters and the regional parliament in September. Dudayev was elected president on 27 October 1991 and declared independence on 1 November. A secular constitution followed in March 1992, and in June 1992 he dissolved parliament and ruled by decree.
Russia invaded on 11 December 1994. The First Chechen War ended after Russia's defeat in the battle for Grozny in August 1996. On 12 May 1997 presidents Yeltsin and Aslan Maskhadov signed a peace treaty in Moscow. Sharia courts, which apply Islamic law, were set up after the war, a sharia-based criminal code was adopted in 1996, and in February 1999 Maskhadov declared an Islamic republic, which parliament said he had no power to do.
The Second Chechen War began in August 1999 and Grozny fell on 6 February 2000. In June 2000 Akhmad Kadyrov took charge of a Russian-backed administration. Recognition was slight. The Taliban recognised Ichkeria in January 2000, and Maskhadov rejected that. Georgia's Zviad Gamsakhurdia, himself then a leader in exile, also recognised it. Estonia voted to do so but never completed the act.
Akhmed Zakayev founded a government in exile in November 2007 and is based in London. On 18 October 2022 Ukraine's parliament declared Ichkeria temporarily occupied by Russia, which falls short of full diplomatic recognition. Armed units under the exile government's name were formed in Ukraine that month. Analyst Mark Galeotti describes the exile government's influence as marginal, and rival factions dispute who speaks for it.
mechanism: A region of a larger state declared independence and defended it by force for most of a decade. Under Russian law it remained part of Russia, and winning one war gave it a treaty but no wide recognition, so nothing stood in the way of a second war.

name: Donetsk People's Republic
anchor: Donetsk, in eastern Ukraine.
founder: Separatists in the Donetsk regional government building
stopped_by: Annexed by Russia in 2022, which most states reject
currency: Russian ruble from 2015, hryvnia in parallel until September 2015
passports: Its own from March 2016; Russian passports issued from June 2019
challenge: Ukraine calls the territory occupied; UN General Assembly condemned the annexation by 143 votes to 5
recognition: Russia, Syria and North Korea, and South Ossetia and Abkhazia, before annexation
story:
The Donetsk People's Republic was declared on 7 April 2014 by separatists gathered in the regional government building in Donetsk, in eastern Ukraine. Ukrainian media reported that no city or district council sent representatives. On 11 May 2014 a referendum in the separatist-held parts of the region was held, and its organisers claimed 89 per cent in favour of self-rule on a turnout of nearly 75 per cent. No government officially recognised the result.
The republic set up a parliament of 100 deputies called the People's Council. The Russian ruble came into official use on 1 January 2015, and it issued its own passports from March 2016. From June 2019 Russia began handing out its own passports to residents, with 470,000 issued across the Donetsk and Luhansk areas by July 2021 according to the Russian official Dmitry Kozak.
Ukraine passed a law on special status for the area in September 2014, declared the republics terrorist organisations in January 2015, and in 2018 declared the territory occupied by Russia. On 12 February 2015 leaders of both republics signed the Minsk II peace agreement, but Ukraine's parliament did not ratify the constitutional changes it called for.
No UN member recognised the republic until Russia did on 21 February 2022, three days before its full invasion of Ukraine. Syria followed in June and North Korea in July 2022. A vote on joining Russia was held on 23 to 27 September 2022, and commentators widely called it a sham. Russia announced annexation on 30 September. On 12 October the UN General Assembly condemned it in Resolution ES-11/4, with 143 votes for, 35 abstentions and 5 against. Russia now treats the area as one of its federal regions, while Ukraine and most states still regard it as Ukrainian.
mechanism: A declared republic won recognition only from the state backing it and that state's allies, and that state then absorbed it. Annexation by force does not change the legal title in the view of most states, which is what the General Assembly resolution records.

name: Luhansk People's Republic
anchor: Luhansk, in eastern Ukraine.
founder: Pro-Russian activists at the regional state administration building
stopped_by: Annexed by Russia in 2022, which most states reject
pop: About 2.1 million estimated before 2022; about 1.4 million in December 2017
challenge: Ukraine claims the territory; UN General Assembly condemned the annexation by 143 votes to 5
recognition: Russia, Syria and North Korea, and South Ossetia and Abkhazia, before annexation
story:
The Luhansk People's Republic was declared on 27 April 2014 by pro-Russian activists gathered outside the regional government building in Luhansk, in eastern Ukraine. They seized the building two days later. A referendum on 11 May 2014 followed. Organisers said 96.2 per cent voted for self-rule on a turnout of 81 per cent, and no international observers were present.
From 2015 to early 2022 the republic held the land between the Russian border and the ceasefire line set by the Minsk agreements, the peace deals signed in 2014 and 2015. Its 2014 constitution did not spell out its borders. It had a 50-seat parliament, and in 2020 declared Russian its only state language. Pensions in 2015 were paid mostly in Russian rubles.
Russia recognised it on 21 February 2022, three days before invading Ukraine, and in doing so accepted the republic's claim to the entire Luhansk region. Syria and North Korea recognised it later that year. No UN member had done so before 2022. Officials reported 98 per cent in favour of joining Russia in a September 2022 vote, and Russia announced annexation on 30 September. The UN General Assembly condemned the annexation on 12 October by 143 votes to 5, with 35 abstentions. Russia treats it as one of its regions, and Ukraine and most other states regard it as Ukrainian territory. Freedom House scored it 2 out of 100 for political rights and civil liberties in 2024.
mechanism: Its path was the same as that of Donetsk. It relied on the backing of a neighbouring state, gained recognition from that state only after eight years, and was then absorbed into it.

name: Bangladesh 1971
anchor: Dhaka, then the chief city of East Pakistan.
founder: Awami League, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, and the Mukti Bahini guerrillas
challenge: Pakistan fought the secession until its troops surrendered on 16 December 1971
recognition: Bhutan first on 6 December 1971, India and most UN members by 1972
story:
Bangladesh is the clearest case since 1945 of a territory breaking away from an established state by war and then gaining general recognition. It was East Pakistan, separated from West Pakistan by India. In the 1970 election the Awami League won 167 of East Pakistan's 169 seats, which gave it a majority of the 313 seats in Pakistan's National Assembly. The West Pakistani politician Zulfikar Ali Bhutto refused to let its leader, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, become prime minister.
On the night of 25 March 1971 the Pakistani army began Operation Searchlight, intended to take the main cities and end opposition within a month. Mujib was arrested. On 26 March independence was declared, with Major Ziaur Rahman reading the declaration on Mujib's behalf over Chittagong radio. A provisional government was formed on 17 April 1971 in what is now Meherpur District, with Mujib as president in absence and Tajuddin Ahmad as prime minister. Bengali soldiers and civilians formed a guerrilla force called the Mukti Bahini.
India entered the war on 3 December 1971 after Pakistani air strikes. Bhutan was the first state to recognise Bangladesh, on 6 December. On 16 December Lieutenant General A. A. K. Niazi signed the surrender, and over 93,000 Pakistani troops gave themselves up. Estimates of the people killed by Pakistani forces and their allies range widely, from about 300,000 to 3,000,000 in the figures usually cited, and independent researchers including The BMJ estimate 125,000 to 505,000 deaths.
Most UN members recognised Bangladesh during 1972, including the Soviet Union in January and the United States in April. China vetoed its UN application in 1972, citing unresolved questions over Pakistani prisoners, and recognised it on 31 August 1975.
mechanism: Pakistan never agreed to the break and international law gave no ready right to secede. The result came from a military outcome, with a neighbouring state's forces, followed by recognition from one state after another.

name: Republika Srpska
aka: Republic of the Serb People of Bosnia and Herzegovina
anchor: Banja Luka, its de facto capital in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
founder: Assembly of the Serb People in Bosnia
pop: 1,228,423 in the 2013 census by one count
currency: Convertible mark, shared with all of Bosnia
challenge: Constitutional Court ruled its 9 January holiday unconstitutional in 2015; its president Milorad Dodik was removed from office in 2025
recognition: A recognised part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not a state
story:
Republika Srpska began as a breakaway Serb state and survives as one half of the country it tried to leave. As Yugoslavia broke up, Bosnia's Serb politicians held a vote in Serb areas in November 1991, with 96 per cent support for staying in a federation with Serbia and Montenegro. On 9 January 1992 their assembly proclaimed a Republic of the Serb People of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it took the name Republika Srpska on 12 August 1992.
The rest of Bosnia voted for independence in a referendum on 29 February and 1 March 1992, which most Serbs boycotted. The European Community and the United States recognised Bosnia in April 1992. The Bosnian War lasted until autumn 1995.
The Dayton Agreement, reached on 21 November 1995 and signed in Paris on 14 December, ended the war. Under it, Republika Srpska became one of Bosnia and Herzegovina's two entities, meaning self-governing halves of one state. It covers 48 per cent of the land and has about 35 per cent of the people. It has its own parliament, president and government, and it uses Bosnia's convertible mark. Sarajevo is its constitutional capital and Banja Luka its working one.
Conflicts with the Bosnian state continue. In 2015 the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina ruled the 9 January holiday unconstitutional. In February 2025 the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina sentenced its president, Milorad Dodik, to one year in prison and a six-year ban from office for not complying with decisions of the international High Representative. The sentence was confirmed in August 2025, ending his term, and Dodik called it political persecution.
mechanism: The peace deal did not grant independence, but it gave the separatist state's government a lasting place inside the state it fought, and a peace treaty secures that place. The claim to full statehood stayed unmet.

name: Republic of Serbian Krajina
anchor: Knin, its capital in Croatia.
founder: Serb regional authorities in Croatia; first president Milan Babić
challenge: Overrun by Croatia in May and August 1995
recognition: None
story:
The Republic of Serbian Krajina was a Serb state declared inside Croatia during the breakup of Yugoslavia. In August 1990 a referendum limited to Serbs passed with 99.7 per cent, and Croatia declared it illegal. In March 1991 another vote favoured joining Serbia and staying in Yugoslavia, and on 1 April 1991 the area said it was seceding from Croatia. Serb regions proclaimed the republic on 19 December 1991, with a constitution the same day and Milan Babić as president. Its capital was Knin and at its largest it covered 17,028 square kilometres.
It had a National Assembly, its own army of up to about 30,000, and its own dinar from July 1992. UN peacekeepers arrived in 1992 and set up four UN Protected Areas under a January 1992 agreement. No country or international organisation recognised it. Croatia's own independence referendum in May 1991 passed with 93 per cent of votes, with many Serbs boycotting.
Croatia took Western Slavonia in Operation Flash in May 1995 and most of the rest in Operation Storm in August 1995. Between 150,000 and 200,000 Serbs fled and about 5,000 to 6,000, mostly elderly, stayed. The last part, in eastern Slavonia, passed to UN administration after the Erdut Agreement of November 1995 and returned to Croatia in 1998.
mechanism: Referendums limited to one ethnic group gave the republic a claim, but the state it left had already been recognised within its old borders, and that left the republic with no international backing when Croatia took the land back.

name: Free Aceh Movement
anchor: Banda Aceh, northern Sumatra, Indonesia.
founder: Hasan di Tiro
challenge: Indonesian military operations; a peace deal in place of independence
recognition: No state
story:
The Free Aceh Movement, known as GAM, was an armed group seeking independence for Aceh, at the northern tip of Sumatra in Indonesia. Hasan di Tiro founded it in December 1976. Its first attack, in 1977, killed an American engineer working for Mobil. By 1979 government units had largely crushed it and di Tiro fled, and its leaders lived in exile in Stockholm for most of the 1980s and 1990s.
Fighting returned in waves. Indonesia declared Aceh a special military operations area in 1989. Total deaths across the whole conflict are estimated at over 15,000. An offensive in 2003 and 2004 reportedly cost GAM about half its members.
On 26 December 2004 a tsunami struck Aceh, and two days later GAM declared a ceasefire so that aid could get in. Talks in Finland began in February 2005, led by the former Finnish president Martti Ahtisaari. The agreement signed in Helsinki on 15 August 2005 ended the war. GAM disarmed, Indonesia withdrew its troops and police from outside the region, about 500 exiled members were given amnesty and about 1,400 prisoners freed. Aceh gained local political parties and kept 70 per cent of income from local natural resources. A joint EU and ASEAN mission monitored it.
GAM disbanded its military wing in December 2005. Di Tiro returned to Indonesia in 2008. Former GAM figures went on to win the governorship in 2006 and 2012.
mechanism: A separatist war ended with a negotiated autonomy deal, which gave up independence in return for local parties, a share of resource income and amnesty, all with outside monitors.

name: Republic of West Papua
anchor: Jayapura, in western New Guinea, Indonesia.
founder: Free Papua Movement; Seth Roemkorem and Jacob Prai declared the republic in 1971
challenge: Indonesia governs the territory and labelled the movement terrorist in 2021
recognition: No state recognises it; Senegal allowed the movement an embassy in Dakar
story:
West Papua is the western half of the island of New Guinea. The Dutch held it after Indonesia became independent and were preparing it for self-rule, with elections and a New Guinea Council in 1961. Indonesia also claimed it. The New York Agreement of 1962, signed by the Netherlands and Indonesia and approved by the UN General Assembly, passed it to Indonesia and promised a vote on its future after seven years.
That vote, the Act of Free Choice, was held from 14 July to 2 August 1969. In place of a poll of all adults, 1,025 Papuan elders were selected and instructed, and they reached a consensus for joining Indonesia. The UN's representative had asked for one person, one vote, and Indonesia refused.
The Free Papua Movement began in December 1963. On 1 July 1971 two of its leaders, Seth Roemkorem and Jacob Prai, declared a Republic of West Papua and drafted a constitution. They soon fell out. The movement has armed units with no single commander, groups inside the territory that hold demonstrations, and leaders abroad who seek international support. Its peak of outside backing was an embassy that Senegal allowed in Dakar. No state recognises the republic.
Indonesia has labelled the movement a terrorist and separatist organisation since 2021. Fighting continues, including the holding of a New Zealand pilot from February 2023 to September 2024 and the shooting of two pilots in February 2026. No political settlement exists.
mechanism: The state's title rests on a treaty and a UN-noted vote, and separatists contest that vote as a real act of choice. With the title accepted by other states, the declared republic has no recognised standing.

name: Iraqi Kurdistan referendum, 2017
anchor: Erbil, capital of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq.
founder: Masoud Barzani and the Kurdistan Regional Government
stopped_by: Iraqi Supreme Court and Iraqi army
challenge: Iraq's Supreme Court ruled that no province may secede; Iraqi troops took Kirkuk
recognition: Israel alone endorsed it; Turkey, Iran and the US opposed the vote
story:
The Kurdistan Region is a self-governing part of northern Iraq with its own government. On 7 June 2017 its president, Masoud Barzani, announced a vote on independence for 25 September. It would also take place in areas outside the region that both Erbil and Baghdad claim, including oil-rich Kirkuk. A Yes was to start negotiations and state-building and did not itself declare a state.
Iraq's parliament rejected the plan on 12 September and the Supreme Court ordered it suspended on 18 September. Barzani went ahead. The official count was 92.73 per cent Yes on a turnout of 72.16 per cent. Turkey warned that Kurdistan would pay dearly and Iran's Supreme Leader called the vote a betrayal. The United States said it supported a unified Iraq. Israel's prime minister backed Kurdish efforts for a state.
Four days later Baghdad stopped most international flights to Erbil and Sulaimaniya, and Iran closed its border. On 15 October Iraqi forces moved on Kirkuk. The Kurdish government lost about 40 per cent of its territory, including the Kirkuk oil fields, its main source of revenue.
On 25 October the regional government offered to freeze the result and talk. Barzani announced on 29 October that he would step down. On 6 November the Supreme Court ruled that no province may secede, and the regional government said it would respect the ruling.
mechanism: A self-governing region held a vote against the wishes of its parent state and neighbours. A large majority gave it no legal effect, since the state's constitution and court rejected secession and the region depended on neighbours for flights and borders.

name: Quebec referendums, 1980 and 1995
anchor: Quebec City, capital of the province of Quebec, Canada.
founder: Parti Québécois; René Lévesque and Jacques Parizeau
laws: Reference re Secession of Quebec (1998); Clarity Act
challenge: Lost both votes; Supreme Court of Canada ruled out unilateral secession
recognition: Accepted as lawful votes by Canada; no state recognition sought after defeat
story:
Quebec is a mainly French-speaking province of Canada. René Lévesque founded a movement for sovereignty-association in 1967, meaning independence combined with an economic partnership with Canada, and in 1968 it merged into the Parti Québécois. The party won provincial power in 1976.
Its first referendum, in 1980, asked for a mandate to negotiate sovereignty-association and was rejected by 60 per cent to 40 per cent. The party returned to power in 1994 under Jacques Parizeau and held a second referendum in 1995, in which negotiating a partnership with Canada was optional. No won by 50.6 per cent to 49.4 per cent, a margin of 53,498 votes out of more than 4.7 million. Parizeau blamed money and ethnic votes, was widely criticised, and resigned.
The federal government then asked the Supreme Court of Canada whether Quebec could leave on its own. In its opinion of 20 August 1998, the court said no under both Canadian and international law. Secession would need a constitutional amendment. International law gives a right of unilateral secession only to peoples under colonial rule or foreign occupation, and to those denied meaningful self-determination inside a state. It also said that a clear vote on a clear question would oblige the rest of Canada to negotiate.
Parliament followed with the Clarity Act, which lets the House of Commons decide whether a question is clear and requires a clear majority. Sovereignists widely reject it as illegitimate. In May 2026 a Léger poll found 32 per cent for independence and 68 per cent against.
mechanism: The 1998 opinion became a widely used statement of the law. A region has no unilateral right to leave a democratic state, but a clear vote creates a duty on both sides to negotiate.

sources.t: Wikipedia, Reference Re Secession of Quebec

name: Cabinda and FLEC
aka: Front for the Liberation of the Enclave of Cabinda
anchor: Cabinda city, in the Angolan exclave north of the Congo River mouth.
founder: FLEC; Ranque Franque proclaimed the republic in 1975
laws: Treaty of Simulambuco, 1885, cited by separatists
challenge: Governed by Angola since 1975
recognition: None stated
story:
Cabinda is a piece of Angola separated from the rest by a strip of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with the Republic of the Congo to its north. It covers 7,290 square kilometres and produces, on conservative estimates, close to 60 per cent of Angola's oil. In 1885, under the Treaty of Simulambuco, it became a Portuguese protectorate, and separatists base their case for self-determination on that treaty.
Separatist groups joined in August 1963 as the Front for the Liberation of the Enclave of Cabinda, known as FLEC. In January 1975 Portugal and the three main Angolan independence movements signed the Alvor Agreement, which treated Cabinda as part of Angola. FLEC was not invited. On 1 August 1975 Ranque Franque proclaimed a Republic of Cabinda at a summit of African states in Kampala. After Angola's independence in November 1975, forces of Angola's ruling movement and Cuban troops entered Cabinda and overthrew the provisional FLEC government.
A low-level conflict continued. In July 2006 a separatist leader, António Bento Bembe, announced after talks that forces were ready for a ceasefire. On 8 January 2010 gunmen attacked the bus of the Togo football team on its way to the Africa Cup of Nations, killing the assistant coach, the team spokesman and the driver, and an FLEC offshoot claimed responsibility.
mechanism: Decolonisation normally keeps the colonial borders. Separatists argue that Cabinda had a separate treaty with Portugal, and the agreement ending Portuguese rule, which FLEC did not sign, included it in Angola.

name: Ambazonia
anchor: Buea, former capital of Southern Cameroons.
founder: SCACUF, with Sisiku Ayuk Tabe as interim leader
currency: AmbaCoin, a cryptocurrency introduced by activists abroad
challenge: War with Cameroon; leaders arrested in Nigeria and sentenced to life on terrorism charges
recognition: No country as of 2026
story:
Ambazonia is the name separatists use for the English-speaking Northwest and Southwest Regions of Cameroon. After the First World War, German Kamerun was split into French and British mandates. In a UN plebiscite on 11 February 1961, voters in British Southern Cameroons could choose union with Nigeria or with Cameroon, with independence not on the ballot, and about 70 per cent chose Cameroon. It federated as West Cameroon on 1 October 1961. A referendum in 1972 replaced the federation with a single unitary state, ending its autonomy.
The lawyer Fongum Gorji Dinka coined the name in the 1980s and announced a Republic of Ambazonia in a 1985 memorandum, for which he was jailed. Other activists made declarations in 1999 and 2006. In November 2016 English-speaking lawyers, students and teachers began strikes and protests. The government cut phone and internet connections in early 2017.
On 1 October 2017 a separatist coalition unilaterally declared independence. At least 17 people were killed in protests afterward. Late in 2017 a large military deployment began a guerrilla war. On 5 January 2018 the Interim Government, including its president Sisiku Ayuk Tabe, was arrested in Abuja, Nigeria, and sent to Cameroon, and in 2019 Ayuk Tabe and followers received life sentences on terrorism charges. Rival leaders inside the movement then disputed who governs.
Militias have enforced a school strike since 2017. By early 2025 infighting and rebel attacks on civilians had increased sharply. The UN Security Council held an informal meeting on the crisis in 2019. No country has recognised Ambazonia.
mechanism: The plebiscite is the basis of the dispute. Separatists argue that voters were never offered independence and that the 1972 change ended what they had agreed to. Cameroon treats the regions as its own, and no state has accepted the declaration.

name: Azawad
anchor: Gao, the temporary capital, in northern Mali.
founder: National Movement for the Liberation of Azawad (MNLA); Bilal Ag Acherif signed the declaration
stopped_by: Allied Islamist groups, then a peace process with Mali
challenge: Pushed out by Ansar Dine and MOJWA by July 2012
recognition: No foreign state; the African Union, ECOWAS, France and the US rejected it
story:
Azawad is the name given to the northern part of Mali, covering about 60 per cent of the country's land, including the regions of Timbuktu, Kidal and Gao. It is thinly populated, with about 1.5 people per square kilometre. The National Movement for the Liberation of Azawad, known as MNLA, is a mainly Tuareg rebel group that began an uprising on 17 January 2012.
With the Islamist group Ansar Dine, the MNLA took Kidal and Gao in March 2012 and Timbuktu in April. On 6 April Bilal Ag Acherif signed a declaration of independence in Gao, with Timbuktu as the intended capital. The African Union said the declaration had no value. ECOWAS, the West African regional body, called it null and void and said it could use force. France and the United States also rejected it.
On 26 May the MNLA and Ansar Dine announced a pact to create an Islamist state, and the MNLA later withdrew. In June, MOJWA and Ansar Dine, both Islamist groups, drove the MNLA out of Gao and Timbuktu, and by 12 July Ansar Dine had overrun its last towns. On 14 February 2013 the MNLA renounced its claim to independence and asked Mali to negotiate. A peace deal, the Ouagadougou Agreements, followed in June 2013, though fighting resumed. A proposed 2017 referendum on autonomy was shelved.
mechanism: The MNLA briefly controlled the land it declared independent, but its allies took that land from it. African states and their organisations refused to accept any change to Mali's borders.

name: Barotseland
anchor: Mongu, western Zambia.
founder: Barotse National Council (the Kuta)
stopped_by: Zambian government; the Litunga did not back the resolution
laws: Barotseland Agreement of 1964, revoked by Zambia in 1969
challenge: Zambia treats it as a province
recognition: No state; joined UNPO in 2013
story:
Barotseland is the historic kingdom of the Lozi people in what is now western Zambia, ruled by a king called the Litunga. In the 1890s its king Lewanika signed concessions with British agents and it became a British protectorate. In 1911 it was merged into Northern Rhodesia as a province.
In May 1964, shortly before Zambia became independent, the Litunga Mwanawina and Zambia's leader Kenneth Kaunda signed the Barotseland Agreement in London, with Britain signing only as a witness. In 1969 the Zambian government passed a bill revoking it. Riots in Mongu between October 2010 and January 2011 over the agreement left two people dead by police fire and many under arrest.
In 2012 the Barotse National Council passed a resolution accepting the agreement's end and saying the kingdom had therefore gone back to its original status. The Litunga did not support it. Barotseland joined the Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization in 2013, and as of 2019 was working to bring a petition to the International Court of Justice.
mechanism: The legal argument treats the 1964 Agreement as the only link between the kingdom and Zambia, so that cancelling the agreement would cut the link. Zambia's law treats it as ended and the area as part of Zambia.

name: Zanzibar
anchor: Zanzibar City, on the island of Unguja, Tanzania.
founder: UK ended its protectorate in 1963; Afro-Shirazi Party after the 1964 revolution
laws: Own president and House of Representatives inside Tanzania
challenge: Tanzania's prime minister said in 2008 that Zanzibar has no sovereignty in the Union
recognition: Part of the United Republic of Tanzania
story:
Zanzibar is a group of islands off East Africa. The United Kingdom ended its protectorate on 10 December 1963 and Zanzibar became an independent constitutional monarchy under its Sultan. On 12 January 1964 a revolution overthrew Sultan Jamshid bin Abdullah, who fled, and a People's Republic was formed, led by the Afro-Shirazi Party. Over 20,000 people were killed, mostly Arabs and Indians.
In April 1964, about three months later, the new republic merged with mainland Tanganyika, and the union was soon renamed the United Republic of Tanzania. So Zanzibar's period as a separate state lasted just over four months.
Zanzibar still has its own government inside Tanzania, the Revolutionary Government of Zanzibar, with its own president, Revolutionary Council and House of Representatives of 81 members. Tanzanian Prime Minister Mizengo Pinda said in July 2008 that there is no such thing as Zanzibar's sovereignty in the Union Government unless the constitution is changed. On 31 July 2010, 66.2 per cent of voters approved a constitutional change to let rival parties form governments of national unity.
mechanism: Two states merged by agreement, and the smaller kept a government of its own inside the union. That arrangement gives it a president and legislature while the union alone holds statehood abroad.

name: State of Anjouan
anchor: Anjouan, an island of the Comoros.
founder: Foundi Abdallah Ibrahim, later Mohamed Bacar
stopped_by: Comorian and African Union troops, March 2008
challenge: Invaded on 25 March 2008
recognition: None; France declined its request to rejoin
story:
Anjouan is a volcanic island of 424 square kilometres in the Comoros, in the Indian Ocean. It joined the State of Comoros when the islands became independent of France in 1975. On 3 August 1997 it declared itself the independent State of Anjouan under Foundi Abdallah Ibrahim. In October 1997 over 99 per cent voted for independence. The island then asked to rejoin France, its former ruler, and France refused.
A constitution was adopted by referendum in February 1998. Ibrahim handed over power in 1999, and army and navy officers staged a coup in August 2001, from which Mohamed Bacar emerged as leader. In 2002 Anjouan rejoined the Comoros under a new Union constitution, and Bacar was elected president of the island.
His term expired in April 2007. Forces loyal to him overthrew the acting president in May, and in June he held an election the Union government had delayed, claiming about 90 per cent of the vote. In July he again declared independence. The African Union applied sanctions, and in February 2008 the Comoros chose force. About 1,500 soldiers, with African Union contingents, landed on 25 March 2008. Bacar escaped to Mayotte, a nearby French territory, by the next day, and France refused him asylum but also refused to extradite him.
mechanism: An island that could not gain recognition offered itself back to its former ruler, and the former ruler declined. The African Union then backed the state's use of force to end a secession.

name: Rhodesia
anchor: Salisbury, now Harare, its capital.
founder: Ian Smith and his cabinet
stopped_by: Lancaster House Agreement, 1979, after the Bush War
pop: 6,930,000 in the 1978 census, of whom about 270,000 were white in 1976
currency: Rhodesian pound, then Rhodesian dollar from 1970
challenge: UN mandatory sanctions from 1966; war with ZANLA and ZIPRA
recognition: None; South Africa and Portugal kept representatives but gave no diplomatic recognition
story:
Rhodesia was a British colony in southern Africa, governed by a white minority of about 6 per cent of the population. On 11 November 1965 the cabinet of Prime Minister Ian Smith issued a Unilateral Declaration of Independence from the United Kingdom, in order to delay moving to black majority rule. The UK called this an act of rebellion, and its governor dismissed Smith's cabinet, which ignored him. Britain ruled out using force.
The UN called on all states to deny recognition, and in December 1966 it made sanctions mandatory, barring purchases of tobacco, chromium, copper, asbestos, sugar and beef. Portugal re-exported goods with false certificates of origin and South Africa refused to observe the sanctions. The US Byrd Amendment of 1971 allowed imports of Rhodesian chromium and nickel. A Royal Navy squadron tried to block oil deliveries through the Mozambican port of Beira. South Africa and Portugal dealt with Rhodesia through accredited representatives, but they opened no embassies, and no state formally recognised it. It became a republic in March 1970 after a referendum among its mostly white voters, 61,130 to 14,327.
The Bush War began in 1966 with insurgents of ZANLA and ZIPRA, the armed wings of the African nationalist parties. After Portuguese rule ended in Mozambique in 1975, the pressure on Rhodesia grew. A deal with some Black leaders in 1978 led to elections that the main nationalist parties did not take part in, and the country was renamed Zimbabwe Rhodesia on 1 June 1979 under Abel Muzorewa. The international community did not recognise it.
The Lancaster House Agreement of December 1979 put the country back under British colonial rule for a short period. Robert Mugabe's party won elections in February 1980 and the country became independent as Zimbabwe on 18 April 1980.
mechanism: Rhodesia controlled its territory fully for 14 years, which shows that effective control alone does not produce statehood in the eyes of other states. The UN asked members not to recognise it, because the minority government denied the majority self-determination.

name: Basque independence movement
anchor: Vitoria-Gasteiz, seat of the Basque government in Spain.
founder: Basque Nationalist Party, founded around Sabino Arana in 1895; ETA from 1959
stopped_by: Spanish Congress refused the Ibarretxe Plan in 2005; ETA dissolved in 2018
challenge: ETA killed 829 people from 1968 to 2010; Spain's parliament refused to debate a plan for free association
recognition: None sought in practice
story:
The Basque Country lies on both sides of the western Spanish and French border. A political movement for a Basque nation began in the 1890s with Sabino Arana, and the Basque Nationalist Party was founded around him in 1895. During the Spanish Civil War, in October 1936, it gained autonomy from the Spanish Republic and José Antonio Agirre became its president. Basque troops surrendered to Franco's Italian allies at Santoña in 1937, and leaders fled abroad, with the exiled government settling in New York during the Second World War.
Students frustrated with that party's moderate position founded ETA on 31 July 1959. Its non-negotiable demand was an independent state across northern Spain and southern France. Between 1968 and 2010 it killed 829 people, including 340 civilians. After Spain returned to democracy in 1978 Basque autonomy was restored, and the Basque Nationalist Party has led the autonomous region for most of the time since the early 1980s. ETA announced a definitive end to armed activity in October 2011, gave up its weapons in April 2017 and said it had dissolved in 2018.
The main legal attempt was the Ibarretxe Plan, named for regional president Juan José Ibarretxe. It proposed free association with Spain on equal terms, with a right to self-determination. The Basque Parliament approved it on 30 December 2004 by 39 votes to 35. On 1 February 2005 the Spanish Congress refused even to debate it, by 313 votes to 29 with 2 abstentions. In 2026 a Basque government poll found 24 per cent support for independence and 37 per cent against.
mechanism: Spain's constitution offers autonomy but no route to leave without the whole country's agreement. A vote in the regional parliament therefore could not change the region's status once the national parliament said no.

name: Kashmir
anchor: Srinagar, in the Kashmir Valley.
founder: Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front led the independence demand in the insurgency from 1989
stopped_by: Indian government; Pakistan favoured groups that wanted merger
laws: Article 370 of India's constitution gave special status until 2019; UN Security Council Resolution 47
challenge: The plebiscite never took place
recognition: Divided among India, Pakistan and China
story:
Kashmir was a princely state, a territory with its own ruler under British supremacy in India. When Britain left in 1947 its Maharaja, Hari Singh, faced an advance by Pakistani tribesmen and soldiers. On 26 October 1947 he signed an instrument of accession to India, and Indian troops were flown in the next day. India called the accession provisional, subject to a reference to the people. Two days earlier, rebels had formed a provisional Azad, or Free, Kashmir government at Palandri.
On 21 April 1948 UN Security Council Resolution 47 called for a ceasefire, withdrawal of Pakistani fighters, a reduction of Indian forces, and then a plebiscite, a vote of all the people, on accession. The ceasefire took effect on 1 January 1949. No withdrawal happened and no plebiscite was held. India withdrew its offer of one in 1954. Today India holds about 55 per cent of the land and 70 per cent of the people, Pakistan about 30 per cent including Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, and China about 15 per cent including Aksai Chin.
In December 1989 an insurgency began in the Kashmir Valley, led at first by the Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front, which sought an independent state. Pakistan later backed groups that favoured merger with Pakistan. By the end of the 1990s more than 30,000 people had died in estimates by historians, and upward of 100,000 Kashmiri Hindus had left in the early 1990s.
Article 370 of India's constitution had given the Indian-held state its own constitution, flag and internal autonomy. On 5 August 2019 a presidential order ended this, and parliament split the state into two union territories, directly under national government, from 31 October 2019. Phone and internet lines were cut and political leaders detained. On 11 December 2023 India's Supreme Court upheld the change unanimously, called Article 370 temporary, and told the government to restore statehood as soon as possible.
mechanism: The status rests on a contested accession and a UN vote that was called for and never held. Independence was not among the options the resolution offered, and the states holding the land do not accept it.

name: Darfur and the Government of Peace and Unity
anchor: Nyala, South Darfur, headquarters of the parallel government.
founder: SLM and JEM rebels from 2003; Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo and the Rapid Support Forces from 2025
currency: Parallel central bank and banknotes from May 2026
laws: Transitional framework of 4 March 2025 dividing Sudan into eight regions
challenge: Sudan's government calls the government fictitious; the African Union says not to recognise it
recognition: No state
story:
Darfur is the western region of Sudan. In February 2003 rebels of the Sudan Liberation Movement and the Justice and Equality Movement (JEM) began attacking government positions, accusing the government of oppressing the non-Arab population. The government used armed militias known as the Janjaweed against them. Estimates of the dead vary. A research centre, CRED, estimated 178,258 to 461,520 excess deaths in January 2010. The UN Security Council referred the situation to the International Criminal Court in 2005.
The rebels asked mostly for autonomy. JEM said in September 2007 that it would move from demanding self-determination to independence if talks failed. Peace deals in 2006 and 2011 promised a referendum on the region's status and created a Darfur Regional Authority. A deal signed at Juba on 31 August 2020 gave signatory groups seats in the national government.
After war broke out between Sudan's army and a paramilitary force called the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the RSF and its allies drafted a founding charter at a conference in Nairobi in February 2025. A transitional framework followed on 4 March and the RSF's commander, Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, announced a Government of Peace and Unity on 15 April 2025. It claims all of Sudan, is based in the Darfur city of Nyala, and says it has a 15-member presidential council and a two-chamber legislature.
By November 2025 it controlled all of Central, East, South and West Darfur, most of North Darfur and West Kordofan. A Future Bank opened in Nyala in January 2026, and a parallel central bank and new banknotes followed in May 2026. Sudan's government calls it fictitious. The African Union told members not to recognise it. Several states, including the US, the UK, Russia, China, Egypt and Saudi Arabia, criticised it, and no state has recognised it.
mechanism: An armed movement that holds a region declared a government for the whole country, avoiding a claim of secession, and built banks and courts to back it. Without recognition, those institutions function only inside the land it holds.

sources.t: Wikipedia, Government of Peace and Unity

name: Republic of the Rif
anchor: Ajdir, its capital in northern Morocco.
founder: Abd el-Krim and Rif tribal representatives
currency: Riffan in law, Spanish pesetas in practice
challenge: Fought Spain and France until surrender on 26 May 1926
recognition: None; France and Spain refused
story:
The Republic of the Rif was declared on 18 September 1921 by tribal representatives in the Rif, a mountain region of Spanish-ruled northern Morocco, during an uprising against Spain. Abd el-Krim led the revolt and became head of state. That summer his forces had defeated a large Spanish offensive at the Battle of Annual.
It was formally constituted in 1923. The National Riffian Council approved a constitution of 40 articles based on popular authority, with a government answerable to a National Assembly and ministers for finance, foreign affairs, defence and the interior. Its capital was Ajdir. An English financier, Charles Gardiner, was hired in 1923 to set up a Bank of the Rif State. The bank was never created and the banknotes he sent never circulated.
France and Spain did not recognise the republic. Envoys went to London and Paris without success, and a letter sent from London on 6 September 1922 asked for admission to the League of Nations. From 1923 Spain used chemical weapons imported from Germany. In April 1925 Abd el-Krim advanced into French Morocco and threatened Fes, and France and Spain formed a joint force in late 1925.
Abd el-Krim surrendered to the French commander Philippe Pétain on 26 May 1926 and the republic was dissolved the next day. Guerrillas fought until 1927. He was exiled until 1947.
mechanism: The Rif's government was organised on the European model and sought League of Nations membership, but the area was treated in law as a protectorate of Spain, and the colonial powers would not treat it as a state.

name: Republic of Ararat
anchor: Near Mount Ararat, eastern Turkey.
founder: Xoybûn, a Kurdish committee; commander Ihsan Nuri Pasha
challenge: Defeated by Turkey in September 1931
recognition: None; Britain and France restricted Xoybûn under Turkish pressure
story:
The Republic of Ararat was a Kurdish state declared on 28 October 1927 near Mount Ararat in eastern Turkey, though some sources give 1928. The Kurdish committee Xoybûn ran it, with Ihsan Nuri Pasha as military commander and Ibrahim Heski leading the civil side. A village near the mountain, Kurd Ava, was named the provisional capital.
Xoybûn appealed to the great powers and to the League of Nations. Britain and France restricted its activities under Turkish pressure, and no state recognised the republic. A wider uprising began in the summer of 1930 and for a time brought more towns under it. Turkish forces defeated it in September 1931 and retook the land.
mechanism: A small armed body held a mountain area and declared a state, with an appeal to the League of Nations as its only legal step. Without outside backing the League's members had no reason to act against Turkey.

name: Republic of Mahabad
anchor: Mahabad, north-western Iran.
founder: Qazi Muhammad
challenge: Iran retook it on 15 December 1946
recognition: None
story:
The Republic of Mahabad was a Kurdish state in north-western Iran, in the area the Soviet Union occupied during and after the Second World War. Qazi Muhammad announced it on 22 January 1946, after a Kurdish People's Government was founded in the town the month before. It relied on Soviet money and supplies, and it used the Soviet ruble.
No state recognised it, and Western powers backed Iran's central government. The Soviet Union promised Iran on 26 March 1946 to leave and withdrew in June. Iran then reasserted its control, and Iranian forces entered Mahabad on 15 December 1946. Qazi Muhammad was hanged there on 31 March 1947 on charges of treason.
mechanism: The republic existed while a foreign army kept Iran's forces out, and it had no independent means of defence when that army left.

name: Republic of South Maluku
anchor: Ambon, the island where it was proclaimed in Indonesia. Its exile government is in the Netherlands.
founder: Former colonial soldiers and other South Moluccan men; Chris Soumokil; later Johan Manusama in exile
challenge: Indonesia took Ambon in November 1950; Soumokil was executed in 1966
recognition: No state; Dutch government does not recognise the exile government
story:
The Republic of South Maluku was proclaimed at Ambon on 25 April 1950 by former soldiers of the Dutch colonial army and other South Moluccan men loyal to the Dutch crown, as Indonesia was turning its federal system into a single state. Indonesian forces blockaded and invaded Ambon, taking the city on 5 November 1950. The government moved to Seram and fought a guerrilla war. Its leader Chris Soumokil was captured in December 1962 and executed on 12 April 1966.
About 12,000 Moluccan soldiers and their families went to the Netherlands, where a government in exile was formed. Most of them expected to return, and in 1968 over 80 per cent of Moluccans there were still stateless. Today about 40,000 people in the Netherlands are counted as Moluccan, and nearly all are Dutch citizens. The Dutch government has not recognised the exile government and has not seriously opposed its activities.
In the 1970s young Moluccans in the Netherlands carried out armed attacks, including train hijackings at Wijster in 1975 and De Punt in 1977, a school hijacking at Bovensmilde in 1977, and the occupation of a provincial building in Assen in 1978. Hostages and hijackers died. No such actions have happened since the 1980s.
The exile government still has a president, and it joined the Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization in 1991. In October 2010 a legal action by its president, John Wattilete, led Indonesia's president to cancel a visit to the Netherlands the next day. Inside Indonesia, three activists were jailed for three years for treason in 2020 for flying its flag.
mechanism: A government in exile can survive long after it has lost the land, on the toleration of its host. Its host does not recognise it, but its members have the rights of any resident there, and that includes the right to sue.

name: Republic of Anguilla
anchor: The Valley, Anguilla, in the Caribbean.
founder: Ronald Webster and Atlin Harrigan
challenge: About 300 British troops were sent in; the island later got what it had wanted
recognition: None
story:
Anguilla is a small Caribbean island that Britain joined administratively with St Kitts and Nevis. The combined territory was given full internal autonomy in 1967. On 30 May 1967 Anguillans forcibly ejected the St Kitts police from the island. A referendum followed, and they declared independence from St Kitts. The leaders, including Ronald Webster and Atlin Harrigan, wanted separation from St Kitts and a return to British colonial rule, with independence as a means to that end.
Talks stalled. A second referendum in 1969 confirmed the wish to separate, and a Republic of Anguilla was declared unilaterally with Webster as president. A British envoy, William Whitlock, failed to settle the matter. In March 1969 about 300 British troops landed in Operation Sheepskin and restored British authority.
The Anguilla Act 1971 confirmed British rule. In 1980 Anguilla formally separated from St Kitts and Nevis and became a separate Crown colony, and it is now a British Overseas Territory.
mechanism: The rebels' aim was to change which government they answered to, and the former colonial power finally agreed. So a declared republic ended with the island getting separation from St Kitts by a British statute.

name: Western Australia secession vote, 1933
anchor: Perth, capital of Western Australia.
founder: Dominion League, Secession League and Western Australian voters
stopped_by: UK House of Commons select committee
laws: Australian Constitution, a UK statute at the time
challenge: The UK Parliament said it could not legally grant secession
recognition: None sought after refusal
story:
Western Australia voted in 1900 to join the new Australian federation. Campaigns to leave began early, and motions were moved in the state parliament in 1902, 1904 and 1906. In the 1920s and 1930s the Secession League and the Dominion League argued that federal policy harmed the state's economy.
On 8 April 1933, on the same day as a state election, 68 per cent of 237,198 voters supported leaving Australia. The governing party lost the election, but the new Labor government sent a delegation to London to ask the British Parliament to act, because Australia's constitution had been passed as a British law. A select committee of the House of Commons met for about 18 months and refused to consider the request, stating that it could not legally grant secession. The Secession League had disappeared by 1938.
Small movements came back later. The mining businessman Lang Hancock founded a Westralian Secession Movement in 1974, and a WAxit party formed in 2016. In an October 2020 poll, 28 per cent of Western Australians supported leaving.
mechanism: A state voted by a clear majority and took its case to the only parliament that seemed able to act. That parliament said it could not act without the rest of Australia, so the result had no legal effect.

name: National Unity Government of Myanmar
anchor: Sagaing Region, Myanmar, where it said in 2025 it would set its headquarters.
founder: Elected members of parliament in the Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH)
currency: NUGPay, a parallel digital currency, and Spring Revolution treasury bonds
laws: Claims authority from the November 2020 election
challenge: The junta declared it illegal and a terrorist organisation in May 2021
recognition: No UN member; European Parliament resolution recognised it as legitimate representative in October 2021
story:
On 1 February 2021 the army of Myanmar seized power after the National League for Democracy had won the 2020 general election. Members elected in that vote formed a committee called the CRPH and said it was the country's lawful parliament. On 16 April 2021 the CRPH named the National Unity Government, including members of other parties and independents, with Duwa Lashi La as acting president and Mahn Win Khaing Than as prime minister. Aung San Suu Kyi and Win Myint were named to posts but were in custody.
It announced an armed wing, the People's Defense Force, on 5 May 2021, and launched a declared defensive war on 7 September 2021. The junta's State Administration Council declared the NUG illegal and a terrorist organisation. In September 2022 the NUG said that the junta had lost control of half the country, a figure that is its own claim. In January 2025 it said it would base its headquarters in Sagaing Region, inside Myanmar, which makes it unusual among governments called exile governments.
Recognition has come from parliaments and not from states. The European Parliament adopted a resolution in October 2021 recognising the CRPH and NUG as legitimate representatives. The Inter-Parliamentary Union treats the CRPH as a legitimate partner in dialogue. No UN member state has formally recognised the NUG. A 2021 deal that involved China and the United States kept Kyaw Moe Tun, appointed in 2020, in Myanmar's UN seat, and the UN rejected the NUG's attempts to replace him. It has offices in the US, the UK, Norway, France, the Czech Republic, Australia and South Korea, which are not recognised diplomatic missions.
The money comes from unusual sources. The NUG reported raising US$42 million by May 2022, mostly spent on weapons and on supporting striking civil servants. About $10 million came from selling a Yangon home linked to the army chief, about $9.3 million from auctioning seized land in Mandalay, and about $10 million in 18 hours from pre-sales of flats on military-owned land. It also sold gem mining rights and issued bonds. In March 2026 it and four ethnic armed groups founded a joint council for a federal democratic union.
mechanism: Its claim rests on a free election, and that makes it a test of whether votes or control decide who speaks for a state. At the UN a compromise left the old ambassador in place and neither side was formally accepted.

name: Free France
anchor: London, where it began. Brazzaville was its capital from 1940 to 1942.
founder: Charles de Gaulle
laws: De Gaulle argued that French authority had collapsed and servicemen had a duty to fight on
challenge: Vichy France held the legal government; de Gaulle was sentenced to death in absence
recognition: UK recognised de Gaulle on 28 June 1940; the Big Three recognised the Provisional Government on 23 October 1944
story:
When Germany defeated France in June 1940, the French government under Marshal Pétain signed an armistice on 22 June. Charles de Gaulle, a junior minister who opposed it, fled to Britain. On 18 June he broadcast over BBC radio asking French servicemen to keep fighting. In a second broadcast on 19 June he said French authority had collapsed. That statement became the legal basis for his claim to lead a government. A parliamentary vote on 10 July made Pétain leader of the Vichy regime, and de Gaulle was later tried in his absence and sentenced to death for treason.
Churchill recognised de Gaulle as leader of the Free French on 28 June 1940. An unusual point is that Free France soon held French territory. The New Hebrides joined in July. Chad's governor, Félix Éboué, pledged allegiance on 26 August, and by the end of November all of French Equatorial Africa was under it. Its capital was Brazzaville from 1940 to 1942. So it was a government based abroad with colonies of its own. By late July 1940 about 7,000 soldiers had joined in Britain, and three-quarters of the French servicemen there had asked to go home.
A French National Committee was formed in September 1941 and the United States gave it Lend-Lease support that November. After Allied landings in North Africa, a French Committee of National Liberation was founded in Algiers on 3 June 1943. It became the Provisional Government of the French Republic on 3 June 1944. Paris was liberated on 25 August 1944, and the Big Three recognised the provisional government on 23 October 1944. Its forces reached 1,300,000 by May 1945. The Fourth Republic replaced it on 14 October 1946.
mechanism: The Vichy government had a parliamentary vote behind it. De Gaulle's claim rested on the argument that it was not free to act, and it succeeded through British backing, control of colonies, and final victory.

name: Dutch government in exile
anchor: London.
founder: Queen Wilhelmina and her ministers
laws: Royal authority, ratified by the States General in 1946
challenge: Germany occupied the Netherlands until 5 May 1945
recognition: Allied governments dealt with it as the government of the Netherlands
story:
Germany invaded the Netherlands on 10 May 1940. Queen Wilhelmina reached London on 13 May aboard the British destroyer HMS Hereward, and the Dutch armed forces surrendered on 15 May, except in Zeeland. The government went with her. She soon dismissed Prime Minister Dirk Jan de Geer after a dispute over collaboration with Germany, replacing him with Pieter Sjoerds Gerbrandy, who served until 1945.
This government had real assets. It controlled the Dutch East Indies until Japan took them and it had a large merchant fleet. On 23 November 1941 it agreed that the United States could occupy Surinam to protect the bauxite mines used for aluminium. In September 1944 it and the Belgian and Luxembourg governments in exile signed the London Customs Convention, a customs union that later became Benelux.
It prepared a military administration to take over after liberation, which began in Maastricht in September 1944. The Netherlands was liberated on 5 May 1945 and the government went home. In 1946 the States General, the Dutch parliament, ratified what the Queen had done as head of the exile government.
mechanism: Because the Queen and the ministers left together, the government kept its unbroken legal claim. Its overseas territories, ships and money meant that it could act like a state, and it signed a treaty that outlasted the war.

name: Norwegian government in exile
anchor: London.
founder: King Haakon VII and Johan Nygaardsvold's cabinet
challenge: Germany occupied Norway and backed Quisling in Oslo
recognition: The Allies treated it as the lawful government
story:
German forces invaded Norway on 9 April 1940. After two months of fighting, the Labour cabinet of Johan Nygaardsvold left on 7 June 1940 and set up in London with King Haakon VII and Crown Prince Olav. It remained the government in law throughout the war, while Oslo had occupation regimes run by the German official Terboven and by Vidkun Quisling, who led a government from 1942 to 1945.
It came home aboard RMS Andes on 31 May 1945. Nygaardsvold announced his resignation on 12 June and the Gerhardsen cabinet took over on 25 June 1945. The word exile did not bring an end to its legal continuity, since the same cabinet that left in 1940 handed over power in 1945.
mechanism: A government that leaves under attack with its head of state can go on being the lawful government from abroad if other states keep treating it as such, even when another regime holds the capital.

name: Czechoslovak government in exile
anchor: London, in Marylebone.
founder: Edvard Beneš
challenge: Munich Agreement and German occupation; had to build its standing step by step
recognition: France and Britain accepted a committee in 1939; Britain, the US and the USSR dealt with it as a government by 1941
story:
The Czechoslovak case shows how an exile government can be built from almost nothing. Under the Munich Agreement of 30 September 1938, Czechoslovakia lost territory to Germany, and President Edvard Beneš resigned a week later. Germany occupied the rest on 15 March 1939. Beneš, by then a private person abroad, created a Czechoslovak National Committee in Paris in October 1939. France agreed that it could rebuild an army on French soil, and France and Britain let it sign treaties in late 1939.
The committee moved to London in 1940 after France fell, and Winston Churchill then recognised Beneš as president. On 18 April 1941 it asked Britain to agree to treaties in the name of the Czechoslovak Republic, and Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden assented on 18 July. The US and USSR followed that year. In 1942, after the assassination of the German official Heydrich in Operation Anthropoid, Britain and Free France repudiated the Munich Agreement, which gave the government a full legal claim to the country's old borders.
It signed a treaty with the Soviet Union in December 1943. In March 1945 key cabinet posts went to Czechoslovak Communists who had been in the USSR, and a new government was formed in Košice on 5 April 1945, ending the exile period.
mechanism: A former president with no office created a committee and asked one state after another to widen what it could do. Recognition came in stages, from running an army, to signing treaties, to being a government, with each step granted by the Allies for wartime reasons.

name: Spanish Republican government in exile
anchor: Mexico City, its base from 1940 to 1946. Paris before and after.
founder: Diego Martínez Barrio and Juan Negrín
challenge: Franco won the Civil War and the great powers did not recognise the exile government
recognition: Mexico, Panama, Guatemala, Venezuela, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Yugoslavia, Romania and Albania just after the war
story:
The Spanish Republic lost the Civil War to General Franco in 1939, and its government left Spain and carried on abroad. It sat in Paris until 1940, in Mexico City from 1940 to 1946, and in Paris again from 1946 to 1977. Mexico under President Lázaro Cárdenas continued to recognise it. In the years just after the Second World War it had diplomatic relations with Mexico, Panama, Guatemala, Venezuela, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Yugoslavia, Romania and Albania. The United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union did not recognise it.
It kept up a line of presidents and prime ministers for 38 years. Franco died in 1975 and Spain moved toward democracy. On 1 July 1977 King Juan Carlos received the exiled leaders in Madrid, and they recognised his government as the lawful government of Spain and formally dissolved their own.
mechanism: The government lasted for as long as a few states kept recognising it, and it ended by its own decision once a democratic government was in place in Spain.

sources.t: Wikipedia, Spanish Republican government in exile

name: Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea
anchor: Shanghai French Concession, its first base.
founder: Korean independence activists after the March First Movement; Syngman Rhee, Kim Ku
challenge: Japan ruled Korea until 1945; the US military administration did not accept it as a government
recognition: No country formally recognised it; the Guangzhou Government of the Republic of China did in 1921
story:
Japan ruled Korea from 1910. After the independence declaration of 1 March 1919 and mass protests, Korean activists formed a provisional assembly and government in the Shanghai French Concession on 10 and 11 April 1919. Groups in Seoul and the Russian Maritime Province merged with it in September. It moved with the war through Hangzhou, Nanjing, Changsha and Guangzhou to Chongqing, its base from 1940 to 1945.
Its assembly impeached its first president, Syngman Rhee, in 1925. It coordinated armed groups, which fought Japanese forces in 1920, and backed an attack on Japanese leaders in Shanghai's Hongkew Park in April 1932. It formed the Korean Liberation Army in the 1940s, with help from the US Office of Strategic Services, and it declared war on Japan and Germany on 9 December 1941. The Chinese Nationalists, the Soviet Union and France gave support.
No country formally recognised it, apart from a rival Chinese government at Guangzhou in 1921. When Japan surrendered in 1945, members came home as private people under US military administration and competed for power. The peninsula was divided in 1948, and Rhee became president of South Korea on 15 August 1948. South Korea's 1987 constitution says the republic succeeds the legal traditions of the provisional government.
mechanism: Without recognition during its life it gained no seat at the peace talks after Japan's defeat. Its later legal role came from a later constitution of the state that followed it.

sources.t: Wikipedia, Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea

name: Provisional Government of the Algerian Republic
anchor: Tunis, its headquarters from 1960 to 1962.
founder: National Liberation Front (FLN); Ferhat Abbas
challenge: France ruled Algeria until 1962
recognition: Morocco, Tunisia, Egypt, other Arab states and Pakistan
story:
The war for Algerian independence from France began on 1 November 1954. On 19 September 1958 the National Liberation Front, known as the FLN, set up a Provisional Government of the Algerian Republic in Cairo, with Ferhat Abbas as president. It moved to Tunis in 1960. Morocco, Tunisia, Egypt, other Arab states and Pakistan recognised it while France still ruled Algeria.
Its purpose was to give the independence movement a body that could negotiate and sign, and it did so. The Évian Accords with France were signed on 19 March 1962 and independence was proclaimed on 5 July 1962. Benyoucef Benkhedda had replaced Abbas in 1961. The government took its seat in Algiers on 1 July 1962, but Ahmed Ben Bella took power through a rival body and it was dissolved later that year.
mechanism: A liberation movement declared itself a government while abroad so that it could seek recognition and negotiate as an equal with the colonial power. That worked with France, but it did not decide who would hold power at home afterward.

sources.t: Wikipedia, Provisional Government of the Algerian Republic

name: Kuwaiti government in exile, 1990 to 1991
anchor: Ta'if, Saudi Arabia.
founder: Emir of Kuwait's government
challenge: Iraq invaded on 2 August 1990
recognition: Treated by other states as Kuwait's government
story: Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990 and its government formed in exile the same day at Ta'if in Saudi Arabia. It returned in March 1991. It is a short case of a government in exile that went back within about seven months.
mechanism: A government pushed out by a neighbour's invasion stayed in place as the lawful authority in the eyes of other states.

name: Provisional Government of Free India
anchor: Singapore, under Japanese occupation.
founder: Subhas Chandra Bose
challenge: Its army was defeated in Burma, and Japanese support ended when Japan surrendered
recognition: Germany, Japan, the Italian Social Republic, the Wang Jingwei Government, Thailand, Burma, Manchukuo and the Second Philippine Republic
story:
India was under British rule during the Second World War. The Indian nationalist Subhas Chandra Bose arrived in Singapore, then held by Japan, on 2 July 1943, and on 21 October he founded the Provisional Government of Free India, called Azad Hind, with himself as head of state. It declared war on the United States and Britain that same night.
Its diplomatic partners were Germany, Japan and governments allied with them, including Thailand, Manchukuo and the Second Philippine Republic. Japan gave it nominal authority over the Andaman and Nicobar Islands late in 1943, and Japanese forces there kept real control. In 1944 Japan shot 44 Indian civilians at Homfreyganj in those islands on suspicion of spying. Its Indian National Army fought in Manipur and Burma and was defeated around Rangoon in 1945.
The government is listed as ending on 18 August 1945, as Japan surrendered and Bose was reported to have died in a plane crash from Taiwan. Afterward 300 of its officers were charged with treason in India.
mechanism: It was a government created on territory held by a wartime ally, and its authority depended on that ally. Recognition came only from one side of the war and ended when that side lost.

name: Second World War governments in London
anchor: London.
founder: Belgian, Greek, Yugoslav, Luxembourg, Albanian and other leaders who fled German and Italian occupation
challenge: Their countries were occupied, and some returned to find a different government in power
recognition: Varied; Britain hosted most, and refused Albania's King Zog
story:
During the Second World War, London became the base for many governments of occupied countries. Norway, the Netherlands, Czechoslovakia, Poland and Free France have their own entries here. Others stayed there too, each on different terms.
Belgium's cabinet under Hubert Pierlot went first to Bordeaux and then to London, from October 1940 to September 1944. King Leopold III stayed behind as a German prisoner, while the government went on running the Belgian Congo. Luxembourg's government moved through Paris and Lisbon to London and Montreal, and it sought recognition as a full Allied member. Greece's government sat in Cairo and London from May 1941 to October 1944 and was recognised internationally, and it merged with a Free Greece body after the Lebanon Conference.
Yugoslavia's government was in London from June 1941. Under the June 1944 Tito-Šubašić Agreements it joined with the Partisans' government, and it ended in March 1946 with the monarchy not restored. King Zog of Albania lived in London and then nearby from April 1939, but the Allies refused to recognise him or work with him, and he abdicated in 1946. An Austrian Office ran in London from August 1941 to May 1945 with British support and no official recognition.
Outside London, Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia lived in Bath from 1936 and returned with British forces in 1941, and the Philippine Commonwealth went to Melbourne and then Washington, D.C.
mechanism: An exile government's standing came from whether its host and the other Allies chose to deal with it. A government with colonies, like Belgium, had resources to use, while those with no assets or Allied support, like Zog, had little beyond a title.
