name: East Turkestan republics and exile government
anchor: Kashgar, where the first republic formed. The exile government is in Washington, D.C.
founder: Rebels at Kashgar in 1933; northern districts in 1944; exiles in Washington, D.C., in 2004
challenge: China treats all support for independence as terrorism, extremism and separatism
recognition: No state recognises independence
story:
East Turkestan is the name that independence movements use for the region China calls Xinjiang. A first East Turkestan Republic formed in 1933 after a rebellion in Kashgar against the Republic of China, and a Hui-led army division put it down in 1934.
A second republic held three northern districts, Ili, Tarbaghatai and Altai, from 1944 to 1949 with secret Soviet help. After the Chinese Civil War, the People's Liberation Army took over Xinjiang in 1949, and that republic ended.
An East Turkistan Government in Exile was founded in Washington, D.C., on 14 September 2004. Beijing strongly opposes independence and applies harsh criminal penalties to its supporters. Most states and international organisations do not use the name officially.
mechanism: Both republics held land only while China was divided by war. Since 1949, the claim has existed as an exile body, and no state accepts it.

name: Navajo Nation
anchor: Window Rock, Arizona, its seat of government.
founder: Treaty of 1868 with the United States; Navajo people
pop: 399,494 enrolled members in 2020; 165,158 living on the reservation
laws: Navajo Nation Code in 26 titles, with its own Supreme Court
challenge: Proposed laws go to the US Secretary of the Interior for review; US Supreme Court ruled in 2023 that the US has no duty to secure its water
recognition: A US federally recognised tribe
story:
The Navajo Nation is the largest Native American land base in the United States, at about 27,400 square miles across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah. Its reservation was set up by treaty in 1868, ratified by Congress the same year, and it reached its present borders in 1934. Federal law treats it as a government within the United States and not as a foreign state.
It has its own three-branch government, set up by a 1989 reform. Its 24-member Council passes laws, an elected president runs the executive, and its courts have a Supreme Court, created under that name in 1985, with ten judicial districts as of 2010. About 180 tribal police officers served in 2023. Its voters have repeatedly rejected a written constitution, and its 110 local chapters gained powers under a 1998 act.
Its powers have real effects and clear limits. In March 2020 it imposed stay-at-home orders and curfews across the reservation during COVID-19. But it must submit proposed laws to the US Secretary of the Interior for review. In Arizona v. Navajo Nation, on 22 June 2023, the US Supreme Court ruled that the federal government has no obligation to secure water for the tribe, although the 1868 treaty reserved water for the reservation.
mechanism: A tribal government holds powers that come from its own existence and from a treaty, and the US Congress and courts decide how far they reach. It has far more legal room than a town, but it lacks control over borders, foreign relations or currency.

name: Nisga'a Final Agreement
anchor: New Aiyansh, in the Nass River valley, British Columbia.
founder: Nisga'a Tribal Council, with British Columbia and Canada
challenge: Challenged in court; the BC Supreme Court upheld it on 19 October 2011
recognition: Part of Canada
story:
The Nisga'a are a First Nation in the Nass River valley of north-western British Columbia, Canada. They pressed land claims for over a century, meeting the province's premier in 1887, forming a Land Committee in 1890, and petitioning the British Privy Council in London in 1913.
In Calder v British Columbia in 1973 Frank Calder and the Nisga'a Tribal Council lost their case. Even so, the Supreme Court of Canada ruled for the first time that aboriginal title, a people's right to land from before colonisation, had existed. That ruling opened the way to modern treaties.
The Nisga'a Final Agreement was signed on 27 May 1998 by Nisga'a leaders and the premier of British Columbia, and by the federal government on 4 May 1999. It came into effect on 11 May 2000. It recognises nearly 2,000 square kilometres as Nisga'a land and reserves water for them. Their government, the Nisga'a Lisims Government, controls the land, including forests and fisheries, and has law-making powers. Hereditary chiefs and matriarchs keep a role in traditional laws.
In 2011 Chief James Robinson and Mercy Thomas challenged the agreement as unconstitutional, especially its self-government and law-making powers. The BC Supreme Court upheld it on 19 October 2011.
mechanism: A treaty with the existing state gives a people a government with real law-making powers that is protected by that state's own courts. It is self-government inside Canada, and it makes no claim to statehood.

name: Guna Yala
anchor: Gaigirgordub and the San Blas islands, Caribbean coast of Panama.
founder: Nele Kantule and Colman, then the General Guna Congress
laws: Act No. 16 of 1953; Supreme Court rulings of 2000 and 2001
challenge: Islands at risk from rising seas by the late 21st century
recognition: A region of Panama, called a comarca
story:
Guna Yala is a self-governing indigenous region on Panama's Caribbean coast, of about 2,300 square kilometres, including many small islands. Its people are the Guna. An 1870 Colombian act recognised them as owners of the land, but that was ignored after Panama broke away in 1903.
In February 1925 leaders from 45 villages meeting at Ailigandi proclaimed a Republic of Tule, and a revolt broke out during Carnival, led by Nele Kantule and Colman. 27 people died. An American named Richard Marsh advised them and wrote the declaration. After mediation by the United States a peace agreement was signed on 4 March 1925 in the presence of the American minister. The Guna gave up their declaration of independence and agreed to follow Panamanian law, and they were promised respect for their customs.
Panama later created a Guna district in 1938, and Act No. 16 of 1953 fixed its boundaries and government. The General Guna Congress is the highest political authority. It meets twice a year, and each community's elected leader, called a sahila, casts a vote. A Supreme Court resolution of 2000 requires the consent of indigenous peoples for projects on their land, and a 2001 ruling confirmed that the region has its own organisation separate from the districts.
The region has 51 communities. Its islands are at risk of becoming uninhabitable by the late 21st century because of rising seas.
mechanism: A short armed declaration of independence led to a treaty with its state, and later to a law creating an autonomous region. This shows a path from a claim of statehood to lasting self-government under the state's law.

name: Greenland home rule and self-government
anchor: Nuuk, the capital.
founder: Greenland voters and Denmark
laws: Home Rule Act 1979; Self-Government Act 2009, section 21
challenge: Depends on a Danish block grant of 4.3 billion kroner in 2024
recognition: Part of the Kingdom of Denmark; a recognised people with a legal route to independence
story:
Greenland was a Danish colony until the Danish constitution of 1953 made it a county of Denmark and gave its people Danish citizenship. After a referendum on 17 January 1979 a Home Rule Act took effect on 1 May 1979. Greenland's parliament gained control of some internal policies, while Denmark kept foreign policy, security and natural resources. Greenland left the European Economic Community in 1985, while Denmark stayed in.
On 25 November 2008, 76.22 per cent of voters backed more self-government. The Self-Government Act of 21 June 2009 added 33 areas that Greenland may take over, including courts, police and natural resources. Denmark keeps citizenship, monetary policy, security, foreign affairs and defence. Greenland has its own offices in Brussels and Washington.
The Act recognises Greenlanders as a separate people under international law. Section 21 sets out a legal route by which Greenland's government can begin a move to independence. Money is the practical limit. Denmark's annual grant was 4.3 billion kroner in 2024, and Danish aid made up over 20 per cent of Greenland's economy from 2019 to 2023.
mechanism: Few secession claims have a legal route written down in advance by the parent state, and Greenland has one. The remaining barriers are about money and defence.

name: Free City of Cracow
aka: Free, Independent and Strictly Neutral City of Cracow
anchor: Kraków, now in Poland.
founder: Congress of Vienna; Austria, Prussia and Russia
challenge: Annexed after the Kraków Uprising
recognition: Created and guaranteed by treaty of Austria, Prussia and Russia
story:
The Free City of Cracow was a small city-state of about 1,189 square kilometres, created on 3 May 1815 at the Congress of Vienna, when Austria, Prussia and Russia divided the Polish lands among them. None of the three would let another have the city, so a treaty made it free and guaranteed by all three. Adam Czartoryski did much of the work on its first constitution.
The 1818 constitution gave it wide autonomy. A Governing Senate held executive power and an Assembly of Representatives made laws. Its population was about 95,000 in 1815 and 146,000 by 1843.
Because the city was a base for smuggling weapons into Russian Poland during the uprising of 1830 and 1831, the three powers tightened their grip. A new constitution in 1833 cut the Senate and Assembly and expanded the powers of the three powers' commissars. A secret treaty of 1835 let Austria annex the city if Polish unrest happened again. Austrian police replaced local police in 1836, and the Austrian army occupied it from 1836 to 1841.
After the failed Kraków Uprising of 1846, Austria annexed the city on 16 November 1846, ending the Free City.
mechanism: A city's freedom created by a treaty among stronger neighbours depends on them, and those same neighbours can withdraw it by another agreement.

name: UN Interim Administration in Kosovo
anchor: Pristina, Kosovo.
founder: UN Security Council
challenge: Serbia considers Kosovo's 2008 declaration illegal
recognition: Created by the Security Council
story:
Kosovo was a province of Serbia. On 10 June 1999 the UN Security Council passed Resolution 1244, which placed it under UN civil administration with an international security presence. The UN Interim Administration Mission in Kosovo, UNMIK, was told to perform basic civil administration, build self-government, keep order, and help refugees return.
UNMIK ran the territory by issuing its own regulations. Its first, on 25 July 1999, said which laws applied. Later that year it chose the laws in force before 22 March 1989. It had four parts, called pillars, run by the UN, the OSCE and the European Union, and it appointed administrators for regions and towns. Local elections were held in October 2000. A Constitutional Framework in 2001 created elected Provisional Institutions of Self-Government, and powers were passed to them.
Kosovo declared independence on 17 February 2008. Serbia called this illegal. The International Court of Justice later found it did not violate international law or Resolution 1244. UN staff were cut by 70 per cent that August, and an EU mission took over police, courts and customs in December. International supervision of Kosovo ended in 2012. UNMIK still exists with few day-to-day tasks.
mechanism: The UN governed a territory that legally stayed part of a state, without that state's control and without granting it independence. Because the resolution left status open, it could continue after the territory declared independence.

name: UN Transitional Administration in East Timor
anchor: Dili, East Timor.
founder: UN Security Council; Sérgio Vieira de Mello
recognition: Created by the Security Council
story:
After a violent period following East Timor's 1999 vote to leave Indonesia, the UN Security Council created the UN Transitional Administration in East Timor, known as UNTAET, by Resolution 1272 on 25 October 1999. For the next two and a half years, the UN itself ran the territory, which had no other government.
Sérgio Vieira de Mello, a Brazilian UN official, led it from 19 November 1999. Its peacekeeping force took over in February 2000 from the Australian-led force already there. In January 2000 the US dollar became the official currency and a Central Payments Office was set up. Australia supplied the largest contingent and Portugal the second largest, and many other states sent troops or police.
UNTAET ended on 20 May 2002, when East Timor became independent. Most of its functions passed to the new government, and its soldiers and police moved to a follow-up UN mission, UNMISET.
mechanism: This was a direct UN government with a fixed goal. It held powers normally held by a state, and it gave them up to a new state when independence came.

name: UN Temporary Executive Authority
anchor: Hollandia, now Jayapura, Indonesia.
founder: UN General Assembly, under the New York Agreement
recognition: A body of the UN General Assembly
story:
The UN Temporary Executive Authority, UNTEA, was set up on 1 October 1962 under the New York Agreement between the Netherlands and Indonesia, to run the former Dutch colony of West New Guinea. It was based in Hollandia and was the first time the UN took direct administrative charge of a territory, in place of only monitoring or supervising it.
It was led first by José Rolz-Bennett of Guatemala, then from 15 November 1962 by Jalal Abdoh of Iran. A UN Security Force of up to 1,500 infantry from Pakistan, with 76 air personnel from the United States and Canada, kept order. On 1 May 1963 UNTEA handed the territory to Indonesia. Later UN administrations in Cambodia, Croatia, Kosovo and East Timor followed the same general model.
mechanism: An international body can hold a territory for a short time as a bridge between one state and the next. Here, the UN stood between a departing and an arriving state for seven months.

name: Free State of Fiume
anchor: Rijeka, now in Croatia.
founder: Treaty of Rapallo between Italy and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes
stopped_by: Italian Fascist coup in 1922, Treaty of Rome in 1924
challenge: D'Annunzio's occupation, then a Fascist coup
recognition: Italy, Yugoslavia, the United States, France and the United Kingdom
story:
Fiume is a port on the Adriatic, now Rijeka in Croatia. On 12 September 1919 the Italian poet Gabriele D'Annunzio entered it with followers and held it for 15 months, and he proclaimed an Italian Regency of Carnaro after talks with Italy failed. On 12 November 1920 Italy and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes signed the Treaty of Rapallo, which created the Free State of Fiume on an area of 28 square kilometres. The United States, France and the United Kingdom recognised it. Italian forces expelled D'Annunzio in late December 1920.
In the first elections in 1921 the Autonomist Party won 6,558 votes against 3,443 for the National Bloc, and Riccardo Zanella became president. On 3 March 1922 Italian Fascists carried out a coup and the elected government fled to Kraljevica. Italian troops entered that month. The Treaty of Rome of 27 January 1924 between the same two states divided the matter and gave Fiume to Italy, with annexation effective on 22 February 1924.
mechanism: A new state created by two neighbours can be ended by the same two neighbours, however clear its recognition and however it voted.

name: Kulangsu International Settlement
anchor: Gulangyu island, off Xiamen, China.
founder: Consuls of Britain, the United States, Germany, France, Japan and others
recognition: Foreign consuls agreed it with China in 1902
story:
Kulangsu, now Gulangyu, is a small island off the port of Xiamen in China. On 10 January 1902 consuls of Great Britain, the United States, Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Denmark, the Netherlands, Sweden-Norway, Japan and others signed a charter there, making it an international settlement, an area run by foreigners on Chinese soil. A Municipal Council was established in January 1903.
Its sanitation and public security methods were applied to Xiamen in the 1920s. When Japan occupied Xiamen in 1938, many Chinese refugees moved to the island. The settlement was abolished in 1943 and Chinese authorities took it back.
mechanism: Foreign consuls and a local council ran the place by treaty rights that China had granted under pressure, without any state owning it outright, until those rights ended in wartime.

name: Manchukuo
anchor: Hsinking, now Changchun, its capital in north-eastern China.
founder: Imperial Japan; Puyi as figurehead ruler
challenge: The League of Nations ruled Japan had broken international law by seizing Manchuria
recognition: Japan, and mostly states aligned with the Axis
story:
Manchukuo was a state set up in north-eastern China under Japanese control. Japan invaded Manchuria after the Mukden incident of 18 September 1931. A council of local figures proclaimed Manchukuo on 18 February 1932 and it was formally established at Hsinking on 1 March, with Puyi, the last emperor of China, as Chief Executive. Japan formally recognised it on 15 September 1932. In 1934 it became a monarchy with Puyi as emperor.
It had its own banknotes and banks, and it bought the Chinese Eastern Railway from the Soviet Union in 1935. It received limited recognition, mainly from states aligned with the Axis. The League of Nations ruled that Japan had broken international law by seizing Manchuria.
The Soviet Union declared war on Japan and invaded on 8 August 1945. After Japan's surrender, Puyi abdicated on 17 August and the state was dissolved.
mechanism: A foreign power created and controlled a government on land it had taken by force and called it independent. The League's refusal is an early example of states declining to recognise a change brought about that way.

name: Islamic State territorial claim
anchor: Raqqa, Syria, its de facto capital.
founder: Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi and the Islamic State group
stopped_by: Iraqi forces, the Syrian Democratic Forces and allies
pop: About 12 million under its rule at the end of 2015
currency: Attempted gold dinar, with little use; its economy ran on US dollars
laws: 2015 penal code enforced by its own councils
challenge: Lost Mosul and Raqqa in 2017 and its last Syrian ground in March 2019
recognition: None; the UN designates it a terrorist organisation
story:
The Islamic State is an armed group that seized large parts of Syria and Iraq. On 29 June 2014 it declared a worldwide caliphate, a state claimed to be the rightful rule over all Muslims, and named Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi as its caliph. Raqqa in Syria was its de facto capital. It reached its largest area in May 2015, and it ruled about 12 million people by the end of that year, on a budget above US$1 billion.
It behaved like a government in some ways. It taxed people, sold oil and ran councils that handled legal matters, and it issued a penal code in 2015 with punishments including floggings, amputations and crucifixions. Its attempt at a gold dinar saw little use. The UN designated it a terrorist organisation, which subjects it to sanctions in every member state, and no government recognised it as a state.
Iraqi forces took Mosul on 20 July 2017, and the Syrian Democratic Forces took Raqqa that October. It lost its last Syrian territory at Al-Baghuz Fawqani in March 2019. Its remaining members operate as insurgent cells, and its African affiliates kept a significant territorial presence as of 2025.
mechanism: It rejected the existing state system and asked for no recognition. Control of land, taxes and courts did not produce a legal state, and all other states treated it as a target of sanctions and force.

name: Gagauzia
anchor: Comrat, southern Moldova.
founder: Gagauz leaders, then the Moldovan Parliament
laws: Law on the Special Legal Status of Gagauzia, 1994
challenge: Constitutional Court struck down parts of the 1994 law on 9 July 2026
recognition: An autonomous region of Moldova
story:
The Gagauz are a Turkic-speaking people in southern Moldova. A Gagauz Republic was declared on 19 August 1990, and Moldova's government annulled the declaration as unconstitutional.
The dispute ended by agreement. On 23 December 1994 Moldova's Parliament passed the Law on the Special Legal Status of Gagauzia, which took effect on 14 January 1995 and covers 1,848.5 square kilometres. It has an elected governor called a Bașkan, who sits in Moldova's government, its own People's Assembly with powers over education, culture, local budgets and taxes, and its own police. It can appeal to Moldova's Constitutional Court against national rules.
The law also says that if Moldova ever decided to unite with Romania, Gagauzia would have a right to external self-determination, meaning it could choose its own status. On 2 February 2014 a regional referendum backed closer ties with Russia and independence if Moldova joined the EU. On 9 July 2026 Moldova's Constitutional Court ruled that regional elections must follow national law and struck down several provisions of the 1994 law.
mechanism: A self-declared republic gave up its claim in return for autonomy written into national law, with a right to leave tied to one named event. The law remains under the state's courts, as the 2026 ruling shows.

name: Hatay State
anchor: Antakya, its capital, in today's Turkey.
founder: Sanjak assembly, with Turkish government backing
stopped_by: Merged into Turkey by its own legislature in 1939
laws: Statute of November 1937 drafted by League of Nations states
challenge: Syrian president resigned in protest; critics called the vote rigged
recognition: Under joint French and Turkish military supervision
story:
The Sanjak of Alexandretta was a district of the French Mandate of Syria, with a mix of Turks, Arabs, Alawites and Armenians. Turkey wanted it when the Mandate ended. Its government coined the name Hatay and raised the issue at the League of Nations, and France, the UK, the Netherlands, Belgium and Turkey then drafted a constitution for the district, which took effect in November 1937.
On 2 September 1938 the assembly proclaimed the Hatay State, under joint French and Turkish military supervision. It had 40 members, 22 of them Turks. On 29 June 1939, after a referendum, the legislature voted to dissolve the state and join Turkey. Critics called the vote rigged, because Turkey reportedly brought in tens of thousands of Turks from outside to register and vote.
France reportedly encouraged the annexation, hoping to keep Turkey from allying with Germany. Syria's President Hashim al-Atassi resigned in protest. The last French officials left Antakya on 23 July 1939, and many Arabs and Armenians fled to Syria.
mechanism: A state can be set up for a short time as a legal step between one ruler and the next. An international statute, a local assembly and a referendum served to transfer land to a neighbour.

name: Bangsamoro
anchor: Cotabato City, its de facto seat, in the southern Philippines.
founder: Nur Misuari and the MNLF; Salamat Hashim and the MILF; Philippine government
challenge: Supreme Court removed Sulu in 2024
recognition: Autonomous region of the Philippines
story:
The Moro are Muslim peoples of the southern Philippines. Nur Misuari founded the Moro National Liberation Front on 21 October 1972, a month after martial law was declared, to fight for a homeland. The Tripoli Agreement of 23 December 1976, brokered by Libya, promised autonomy, and an Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao was created in 1989. A breakaway group, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, led by Salamat Hashim, kept fighting.
The government and that group signed a Comprehensive Agreement on 27 March 2014. President Duterte signed the Bangsamoro Organic Law on 26 July 2018, and voters approved it in January and February 2019. The new government was inaugurated on 29 March 2019, with the former rebel leader Murad Ebrahim as chief minister.
The region has a Parliament mandated at 80 members, a chief minister and cabinet, Shari'ah courts for Muslims which non-Muslims may choose to use, and powers to levy its own taxes. The law states that it remains an inseparable part of the Philippines. On 9 September 2024 the Philippine Supreme Court mostly upheld the law but ruled that Sulu is not part of the region, because a simple majority of its voters opposed joining in 2019.
mechanism: Rebels with an independence goal made peace in return for an autonomous parliament, courts and tax powers. Each area joins by its own plebiscite, so its borders depend on local votes.

name: Republic of Crimea, 2014
anchor: Simferopol, Crimea.
founder: Supreme Council of Crimea and Russia
stopped_by: Absorbed into Russia one day after independence
challenge: Ukraine's Constitutional Court ruled the referendum unconstitutional; the UN General Assembly declared it invalid by 100 votes to 11
recognition: Russia, by decree on 17 March 2014
story:
Crimea is a peninsula on the Black Sea that was an autonomous republic of Ukraine. On 26 February 2014 armed men took over its parliament and government buildings. While troops occupied the building, on 27 February, the parliament voted to hold a referendum and dismissed the regional government. Ukraine's interim government declared the votes illegal.
On 11 March the Crimean parliament said it would declare independence and ask to join Russia if voters agreed. On 14 March Ukraine's Constitutional Court ruled the referendum unconstitutional. It was held on 16 March, with official results of about 95.5 per cent for joining Russia on 83 per cent turnout. A report by Evgeny Bobrov suggested these were inflated, estimating 50 to 60 per cent support and 30 to 50 per cent turnout.
On 17 March Crimea declared itself the independent Republic of Crimea, and President Putin recognised it as a sovereign state by decree the same day. On 18 March the treaty for its accession to Russia was signed. On 27 March the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 68/262, which is not binding, by 100 votes to 11 with 58 abstentions, calling the referendum and the change of status invalid.
mechanism: The state existed for a day or so, long enough to sign a treaty joining another state. Russia's action was framed as a merger of two sovereign states, and most states have rejected that framing.
